React only renders a component again when you call `setState`. If you assign to `this.state` or to something inside it, the screen keeps showing the old value, and the next `setState` may overwrite your change.

The constructor is the one place where you can assign `this.state`, because nothing has rendered yet.

{/* Generated by src/codegen/lint-rule-docs.ts. Do not edit this section. */}

## Configure

Off by default. To turn it on:

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"react/no-direct-mutation-state" = "error" # or "warn"
```

{/* End of the generated section. */}

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad {"count": 2} */}
```jsx
class Counter extends React.Component {
  increment() {
    this.state.count++;
  }

  rename(name) {
    this.state.user.name = name;
  }
}
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```jsx
class Counter extends React.Component {
  constructor(props) {
    super(props);
    this.state = { count: 0, user: props.user };
  }

  increment() {
    this.setState(state => ({ count: state.count + 1 }));
  }

  rename(name) {
    this.setState(state => ({ user: { ...state.user, name } }));
  }
}
```

A callback in the constructor runs later, so an assignment there is reported:

{/* bad */}
```jsx
class Counter extends React.Component {
  constructor(props) {
    super(props);
    props.store.subscribe(() => {
      this.state.count = props.store.count;
    });
  }
}
```
